ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, S.C. 2000, c. 17 (PCMLTFA), as amended; Quebec Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, C.Q.L.R. c. P-44.1 (transparency/UBO declaration regime); Quebec Business Corporations Act, C.Q.L.R. c. S-31.1 (QBCA); Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 (Part XII.2 proceeds of crime for the criminal organization and money-laundering offences); United Nations Act, S.C. 2000, c. 42; Special Economic Measures Act, S.C. 1992, c. 17; FINTRAC Regulations under the PCMLTFA.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_disclosure_level: Government_Only_Access: the Quebec transparency register is filed with the Registraire des entreprises du Quebec and is accessible to government authorities, registered financial institutions, and certain accredited persons; it is not a fully public open-search register of ultimate beneficial owners

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, officers, shareholders at the 25% threshold, UBOs, and authorized signatories against the UN Consolidated List as implemented under the United Nations Act, Canadian lists under the Special Economic Measures Act and the Criminal Code (Part II.1), and any FINTRAC-derived domestic watchlists; mandatory enhanced due diligence for domestic and foreign politically exposed persons under PCMLTFA ss. 9.1-9.8; voluntary but strongly advised supplemental OFAC SDN screening given USD Swift Wire and PayPal rails; all screening results and rebuttals must be documented and retained in the AML/CFT compliance file.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Quebec (REQ) - online portal at registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Charter of the French Language (R.S.Q. c. C-11) and the QBCA, the corporate name must be in French or contain a French version; where a non-French name is desired, the French form must be equally prominent; transliteration into the Latin script is mandatory for all registered names; a purely non-French name is generally refused unless supported by a registered trademark or a recognized phonetic necessity
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Tokens implying the Crown or public authority
Tokens contrary to public order or statutory prohibitions
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Extension: file a renewal request online with the REQ before expiry, paying the applicable fee; reservation may be renewed repeatedly. Rejection appeal: (i) within 30 days of the refusal, file a written reconsideration request with the REQ supported by trademark-registry search results, prior-rights evidence, and proof of distinctiveness; (ii) if the refusal is maintained, apply to the Superior Court of Quebec under s. 7(4) QBCA for an order directing the Registraire to register the name; (iii) alternativel, elect a new name or adopt a distinctive element and file fresh articles; rectification of the name may be effected after incorporation at an extra statutory filing cost.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Virtual office and corporate domiciliation services are accepted in Quebec provided that a real physical street address in Quebec is designated as the registered office for service of process by the REQ, the Canada Revenue Agency, and court officials; a post office box alone is prohibited. For this import/trading wholesale business, a virtual office satisfies the incorporation requirement, but Quebec permanent establishment/tax nexus must be reassessed if inventory, employees, or key management functions are established in Quebec.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low risk: less than 5% probability per fiscal year of an unannounced REQ inspection of the registered office for a low-risk wholesale importer of this profile; Canada Revenue Agency compliance visits are estimated at approximately 1-2% annually for such businesses; no FINTRAP high-cash or real-estate trigger elevated risk.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as the central monetary authority; the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) regulates federally chartered banks; FINTRAC administers AML/CFT obligations; in Quebec, the Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF) supervises financial services and money-services businesses.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains a fully liberalised and freely convertible currency for both current-account and capital-account transactions under the Currency Act and the Bank of Canada Act. There are no exchange controls, no prior approvals for foreign investment, and no restrictions on the repatriation of profits, dividends, interest, or capital for non-resident shareholders, provided all applicable federal and Quebec corporate and withholding tax returns are filed and paid. Dividends paid by a Quebec-resident corporation to non-residents are generally subject to Part XIII withholding tax, reduced by treaty where applicable. Capital inflows and outflows must comply with FINTRAC large-transaction reporting thresholds and the Investment Canada Act if the acquisition of control of a Canadian business is involved.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: None. Canada imposes no statutory timeline, no mandatory percentage, and no obligation to surrender export receipts or convert them into Canadian dollars. Export proceeds may be retained in foreign currency in domestic or offshore accounts, and may be used directly for foreign supplier payments, subject only to the exporter's internal tax and financial reporting policies, GST/HST zero-rating documentary requirements, and applicable FINTRAC reports for transactions at or above C$10,000.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.bank_name: Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) – Royal Bank of Canada business account
Bank of Montreal (BMO) – BMO Business Banking
Bank of Nova Scotia (Scotia Bank) – Scotiabank Business Banking
National Bank of Canada (Banque Nationale du Canada) – Business Banking

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium. Foreign fintech or electronic-money institutions (EMIs) without a Canadian registration are not permitted to provide banking or money-transfer services to a Canadian business as a principal regulated entity. They may operate only through a registered Canadian money-services business (MSB) or through a partnership with a schedule I bank. As cross-border virtual issuers, many foreign EMIs will not provide CAD-denominated accounts to non-resident corporate clients, and Quebec requires money-services businesses using an establishment in Quebec to obtain an AMF licence. For the current low-risk die-cast collectibles business, a foreign EMI may be used solely as an auxiliary disbursement rail for small international supplier payments, but the primary operating and escrow account must remain at a tier-1 domestic bank.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical presence for directors is not a statutory requirement under federal or Quebec law. Remote account opening is permitted under FINTRAC/OSFI guidance using corporate registration, certified identification, and electronic signature, but many tier-1 banks require at least one director or UBO to attend an in-person or video identity verification interview during onboarding. For a new exporting corporation with a non-resident shareholder, the recommended approach is to have a local director or authorized signatory physically appear at the Quebec branch for the initial KYC interview, submit original notarised corporate documents, and demonstrate physical operational presence. If remote opening is preferred, the bank will perform EDD and may request external counsel confirmation of the corporate and beneficial-ownership structure.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: UBO ambiguity created by foreign corporate shareholders or trust structures
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Notarised corporate register excerpt, official certificates of incumbency and good standing, a full UBO chain traced to individuals, passports, utility bills and identity documents for all persons with 25% or more ownership, and a board resolution identifying the reporting UBO for each corporate shareholder.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unusual inbound wire volumes or frequent matching inbound/outbound transfers without underlying trade documentation
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Signed commercial invoices, bills of lading, customs declarations, shipping contracts, purchase orders from overseas suppliers, die-casting and tampo-printing production manifests, and bank trail explanations linking each wire to a specific trade transaction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-risk counterparty or jurisdiction in the supplier or distributor network
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Sanctions screening clearance reports from a commercial screening tool, counterparty beneficial-ownership certificates, independent correspondence showing the business purpose, and a written AML risk assessment with EDD file containing evidence of the counterparty's commercial registration and trade history.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Resale of finished products via marketplaces and card processors with settlement mismatches
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Marketplace settlement reports, PayPal merchant statements, e-commerce tax certificates, and reconciled CSVs showing gross sales, transaction fees, FX conversion rates, and net remittances attributed to each customer order.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Naming mismatch between corporate registration, invoicing entity, and bank account title
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certificate of incorporation from Corporations Canada or Registraire des entreprises du Québec, GST/HST registration certificate from CRA, a formal name booking confirmation, and a board resolution confirming the exact operating and invoicing legal name.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity and shareholder-loan injections should be routed by SWIFT wire to the bank account in the name of the Canadian operating company. The wire must clearly specify the sender as the shareholder or shareholder entity, the beneficiary as the Quebec corporation, and include a purpose code reflecting 'Direct Investment in Canada' or 'Intra-company Financing'. The bank will require a board resolution approving the capital contribution or loan, a signed subscription agreement, and, if applicable, a loan agreement with an arm's-length interest rate and repayment schedule. Transactions equal to or above C$10,000 are reported to FINTRAC as large cash or wire transactions; the bank may also require a source-of-wealth questionnaire for the investor. No CFIUS-type foreign investment approval is required for this scale-model manufacturing company, but Investment Canada Act notification thresholds remain applicable if the acquirer is a non-resident investor seeking to acquire control of a Canadian business.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound supplier payments and trade settlements should be executed primarily via SWIFT MT103 as direct wire transfers for invoice settlement, or through a commercial documentary letter of credit (L/C) for larger or contractually governed purchase orders from Chinese die-casting tooling suppliers and tampo-printing vendors. The standard rails are: (1) SWIFT MT103 for straightforward payment against commercial invoice, with the invoice number and contract reference in the payment narrative; (2) SWIFT MT700/Irrevocable Documentary Credit issued by the Canadian bank in favour of the overseas supplier, covering cost, insurance, and freight (CIF) shipments with presentation of a clean bill of lading, commercial invoice, packing list, and certificate of origin; and (3) PayPal as a low-value prompt-payment rail for sample orders, pre-production prototypes, and marketplace refunds. For all inbound and outbound wires, the company must retain underlying trade documents to substantiate the business purpose and ensure consistency with bank AML expectations.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Outright CAD/USD forward currency contracts with a licensed Canadian bank or qualified derivatives counterparty
Non-deliverable forward (NDF) contracts – permitted when the counterparty is required by an offshore bank, although CAD is fully deliverable and such instruments are not generally required
Cross-currency swaps (CAD/USD and CAD/CNY) for longer-dated funding or commercial commitments
FX options and collars on CAD/USD or CAD/CNY for downside protection on large export or import payments
Foreign exchange spot transactions executed at the bank's quoted rate for immediate settlement

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% combined general non-CCPC rate (federal 15% + Quebec 11.5%); qualified manufacturing and processing profits attract the federal M&P rate of 13%, yielding a combined headline rate of 24.5% before Quebec M&P credits and deductions.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory tax holiday for die-cast collectibles; applicable preferences include the federal Manufacturing and Processing Profits deduction (reduces federal rate from 15% to 13%), Quebec M&P rate reduction, accelerated Capital Cost Allowance (Class 43 and Accelerated Investment Incentive), and refundable/non-refundable provincial investment tax credits for qualifying tooling, robotic, and digital printing equipment.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal); filed electronically with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) using Corporation Internet Filing via certified software/EFILE through My Business Account.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; each fiscal period not exceeding 53 weeks.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due no later than 6 months after the corporation’s fiscal year-end; for non-resident corporations carrying on business in Canada, the same 6-month rule applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, business number (BN), provincial registration, mailing address, fiscal period end, jurisdiction of incorporation.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mark the return as a non-resident corporation; state Canadian permanent establishment (PE) location and treaty-residence jurisdiction; attach agent for service details if required by provincial law.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net income computed under GAAP adjusted for tax; taxable income after loss carryovers and deductions (e.g., section 18 adjustments, capital gains reserves).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only report Canadian-source active business income effectively connected with the Canadian PE; transfer pricing adjustments under section 247 must be applied before arriving at taxable income.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Part I Tax and Schedule 1 (M&P Deduction)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal Part I tax calculation on taxable income, including the manufacturing and processing income deduction and general tax reduction.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: M&P relief is available only where the non-resident’s Canadian PE actually engages in qualifying die-casting and tampo printing; document production activities, wages, and machinery utilization.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of federal taxable income among provinces based on gross revenues, wages/salaries, and PE contracts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For Quebec PE, source the proportion of gross sales attributable to Québec customers and employees; attach equivalent Quebec calculation to the CO-17.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculation of tax payable, instalment credits, refunds, and balance remittance.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations must remit balance-due amounts within two months of year-end unless a treaty provision modifies collection; CRA may require security for non-residents under section 220.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty under s.162(2): 5% of unpaid balance plus 1% per complete month up to 12 months; repeated failure to file increases the penalty to 10% plus 2% per month; gross negligence penalty under s.163(2) reaches 50% of the understated tax; daily compound interest accrues on unpaid amounts.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: CO-17 Quebec Corporation Income Tax Return; filed electronically with Revenu Québec via suo (Échange de Données Normalisé / CLIC Revenu Québec XML transmission).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual; follows the same fiscal period as the federal T2 return.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Due within six months after fiscal year-end; final balance due generally no later than two months after year-end for non-CCPC corporations (three months for CCPCs).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quebec enterprise number (NEQ), legal name, actuar/Avant? Civil address, QST account identifier, business activity code.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Provide all identifiers with the Quebec PE status; request a Quebec business number (NEQ/RQ account) before filing; identify the nature of warehouse/manufacturing presence in Quebec.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Taxable Income and Quebec Business Income
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross taxable income, adjustments, and net income subject to Quebec’s corporation tax.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Take the federal taxable income computed for the Canadian PE, then allocate the Quebec share using the CO-17 formulas; arm’s length transfer-pricing records under Quebec Taxation Act must be retained.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Calculation of the Quebec manufacturing and processing tax-rate reduction, including eligible production employees, production equipment, and Ontario? adjustment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only qualified active die-casting and tampo printing activities performed at a Quebec permanent establishment qualify; the non-resident must maintain payroll and machine-hour records to support the reduction.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of taxable income to Quebec based on gross sales, wages, and PE gross book value.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident with PEs in more than one province, the Quebec allocation fraction must be completed in accordance with the Canada-Quebec Agreement? and cited in interprovincial notes; support with invoices, transfer-pricing documentation, and payroll registers.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Non-refundable and refundable credits, instalment credits, and net balance payable/refundable.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Credit claims require a treaty-protected Form NR301? No: an actual Quebec tax-return attachment describing ownership and OECD compliance; remit any balance due with the CO-17 by the statutory due date.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty under the Quebec Taxation Act is 5% of the unpaid provincial tax plus 1% per month up to 12 months; repeated failure attracts a 10% penalty plus 2% monthly; gross negligence penalty equals 50% of the understated provincial tax; daily compounded provincial interest applies; unregistered, non-filing corporations also face administrative late-PIA? (penalty for failure to report business start) and director liability.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% (flat federal Part XIII withholding tax on any dividend paid or credited by a Canadian-resident corporation to a non-resident recipient; Quebec imposes no separate dividend withholding tax).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To obtain a reduced DTA rate (typically 5% for corporate parent owning 10% or more, or 15% for portfolio dividends), the non-resident recipient must deliver to the payor (i) a valid Tax Residence Certificate (TRC) from its country of residence, (ii) a beneficial owner declaration, and (iii) CRA Form NR301 (Waiver of Part XIII Tax) approved in advance; if the payer has already withheld 25%, the non-resident may file CRA Form NR7-R for a refund of the overwithheld amount after the tax year.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory rate: 25% for IP royalty and debt interest paid to non-residents; applicable treaty rates vary, with many Canadian DTAs limiting royalties and interest to 0%–10% (interest often 10% for non-arm’s length; royalties typically 10% for industrial/commercial or 15% for copyright-related payments), conditional on arm’s length character and beneficial ownership.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: CAD 1,000,000 (aggregate annual related-party cross-border transactions requiring Form T106 and transfer-pricing documentation); Country-by-Country Report threshold is CAD 750 million consolidated group revenue.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not maintain a UAE-style ESR regime; however, CRA and Revenu Québec apply the OECD-derived general anti-avoidance rule (s.246? actually s.245 ITA), sham doctrine, treaty shopping rules, and BEPS MLI prohibitions in order to disregard structures lacking real economic substance or valid business purpose; a Quebec-resident die-cast subsidiary must perform actual manufacturing, carry employees, hold tangible equipment, and exercise genuine administration in Canada to access treaty benefits.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Falsifying T2/CO-17 returned amounts, suppressing die-cast unit sales, hiding cash payments through PayPal/Swift transfers into offshore accounts, or claiming M&P relief for non-existent Quebec manufacturing operations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Criminal prosecution under s.239(1) ITA and s.80 Penal Fines? Quebec: fine between 50% and 200% of the tax sought to be evaded plus imprisonment up to five years; disgorgement and compound interest to CRA/Revenu Québec; civil gross negligence penalty of 50% of the understated tax under s.163(2) ITA and corresponding provincial provision.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false returns or direct underreporting face personal civil restitution, CRA asset seizure, prohibition order, travel bans, and imprisonment; where a director personally benefits from diverted corporate cash, the corporate veil is pierced and personal liability attaches to all federal and provincial taxes, penalties, and interest.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Non-Filing or Failure to Register a Quebec Permanent Establishment
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A foreign-related manufacturer sells die-cast goods through a Quebec warehouse, agent, or consignment stock and fails to register with Revenu Québec, files neither T2 nor CO-17, and allocates zero income to Quebec.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Reassessment on attributable net income at the general combined rate; late-filing penalties (5% + 1%/month to 12%) on both federal and provincial tax; involuntary dissolution risk for provincial registration; non-resident deemed-payment assessments relating to amounts withheld on payments to third-party agents.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be jointly and severally liable for unremitted GST/HST and QST under comparable Canadian provisions; for source withholding defaults the CRA issues s.227.1(1) director’s liability notice, authorizing seizure of personal bank accounts, freezing, and, upon ex parte court proceeding, director travel restrictions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Manipulation and Shell IP Parking
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Selling die-cast dies, industrial moulds, or tampo-print software to the foreign parent at below market value, paying excessive management fees, or parking brand IP in a zero-substance Caribbean holding company while the Quebec subsidiary pays royalties and earns thin profits.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Section 247(2) ITA recharacterization of the actual transaction to arm’s length; s.247(3) adjustment of gross income; s.247(4)- penalty of 10% of the amount of adjustment if documentation inadequately prepared; denial of deductions for royalties acquired with an anti-avoidance purpose; gross negligence penalty 50%; provincial parallel penalty under Quebec Taxation Act.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: A director who causes the company to enter into TP arrangements without contemporaneous records can be assessed the TP penalty directly as a remittance officer; if the adjusted tax is not paid, CRA may pursue director liability using an LL? / de facto director determination, seize personal property, and impose a court-ordered travel ban where economic interest is hidden offshore.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Anti-Money Laundering and Beneficial Ownership Mouthwash
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a nominal Quebec subsidiary with nominee directors, opaque shareholders, no physical plant, and no bank activity except receiving inbound Swift wire transfers and PayPal payments for collectible sale commissions, while failing to file FINTRAC reports for cash transactions and mandated beneficial ownership records.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: FINTRAC record-keeping penalty for corporations up to CAD 500,000 per administrative monetary penalty (AMP); repeated/aggravated offences up to CAD 1,000,000 and imprisonment of up to five years for criminally negligent money laundering under the Criminal Code; federal tax evasion penalties as above; Quebec separate AMP for missing registry filings.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly use the shell to launder sale proceeds face criminal charges as principals, personal fines under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, confiscation of personal assets derived from the offence, and extradition/travel restrictions; nominee directors are not shielded merely because they acted at the instruction of the foreign beneficial owner.
